results.summary: This analog design implements an adaptive exponential integrate-and-fire neuron using DPI circuits in the subthreshold regime. It is configured through analog bias voltages that are set by an SPI register, allowing tuning of neuron parameters. The neuron communicates via request and acknowledge handshake signals (NN_req and NN_ack) and includes a multiplexer for selecting internal signals. Documentation is minimal, providing only a brief description without detailed testing procedures or measured results.

This Verilog project is a modified VGA checker pattern generator that outputs standard VGA signals. It is based on the Tiny Tapeout VGA template, with changes made to reverse the direction and alter the default colors. To use it, one connects the outputs to a VGA display and observes the generated graphics. The project is notable for being a simple template derivative intended for experimentation with VGA output on Tiny Tapeout.

This Verilog design implements a memory built-in self-test (MBIST) controller with built-in self-repair (MBISR) for an embedded 256x8-bit SRAM. It uses the March C- algorithm to detect faults and can remap faulty addresses using CAM-based repair, providing DONE and FAIL status outputs. The system automatically tests and repairs the memory on-the-fly, making it suitable for reliable memory subsystems. The documentation is limited to a brief description, with no external testing details or results provided.

This is a basic 4-bit processor implemented in Verilog, featuring a simple instruction set and 16 words of on-chip RAM. It accepts an 8-bit input (4-bit opcode and 4-bit operand) and outputs a 4-bit program counter and a 4-bit value from the accumulator. The processor is intended to be controlled by an external microcontroller like an Arduino, which supplies program instructions and may generate the clock. Testing requires writing a small program and feeding it via the microcontroller, but the documentation notes that testing procedures are not yet finalized.

This mixed-signal design is a 31-stage ring oscillator with controllable current sources, providing divided clock outputs. It is enabled via a ring_enb signal, and when ui_in is set to 0xFF, the oscillator runs and produces divided frequencies on the outputs. The design includes analog control pins for current sources and power, and it can be tested with an oscilloscope to measure timing. The documentation is brief, indicating it was created for the TTIHP26a shuttle, but lacks detailed test results or application notes.

This mixed-signal design is an 8-phase buck converter controller with integrated bias and reference generation, including an ultra-low-power bandgap. It manages startup sequencing, soft-start, phase rotation, and digital configuration through a digital block, while analog blocks implement the regulation loop and generate control signals. The design includes level shifters and interfaces such as an SPI-like serial interface for configuration. Testing requires verifying both digital sequencing and analog control interactions, but the documentation provides no measured results or detailed test setup.

This SystemVerilog project is a digital recreation of the MOS6581 SID sound chip, supporting most of its original features. It is configured via a 4-wire SPI interface and outputs a 1-bit PDM audio signal at 10 MHz. To use it, one connects an SPI master and a low-pass reconstruction filter to the PDM output, then programs voices using registers to generate tones. The design includes a CocoTB test suite and is notable for bringing a classic synthesizer chip to Tiny Tapeout.

This Verilog design is a 2-digit countdown timer that counts down in minutes from a user-set value. It uses a 100 kHz clock, and after the switch is flipped, it decrements the display every 6,000,000 ticks (one minute) until reaching zero. The design drives a multiplexed 7-segment display and includes inputs for a button and switch to set the time. It can be tested in the Wokwi simulation, and requires external hardware such as a common-cathode 7-segment display, a button, and a switch.

This SystemVerilog design implements a true random number generator that harvests entropy from the jitter of free-running ring oscillators. It outputs an 8-bit random byte after whitening the sampled bitstream to remove bias. The module uses a handshake protocol with ready/valid signals to indicate when data is available. Testing involves streaming bytes to a host PC and running statistical tests like NIST SP 800-22, requiring a Tiny Tapeout demo board and an RP2040 microcontroller for data capture.

This VHDL design appears to be a digital phase detector based on the DDMTD (Digital Dual Mixer Time Difference) technique, with inputs for reference and feedback clocks and outputs for phase error. It includes selection pins for gain settings and a bring-up mode, suggesting it is intended for clock synchronization or measurement applications. However, the documentation is essentially absent, providing no explanation of operation or testing. The design is likely an experiment or test, but its exact functionality cannot be determined from the available information.
